findings.title: Every borrower flagged 'Goes negative on timing, not shortage' saw the loan go bad
findings.statement: Real outcomes, not simulation: among the 682 accounts with a loan, 100% of the 19 flagged 'Goes negative on timing, not shortage' ended with the loan in trouble (status B or D) versus 9% of the other 663.
findings.caveat: Small groups for some flags; loan status is a snapshot at end of 2025; flags and loan trouble share causes.

findings.title: No borrower flagged 'Never negative, yet fails a layoff' saw the loan go bad
findings.statement: Real outcomes, not simulation: among the 682 accounts with a loan, 0% of the 389 flagged 'Never negative, yet fails a layoff' ended with the loan in trouble (status B or D) versus 26% of the other 293.
findings.caveat: Small groups for some flags; loan status is a snapshot at end of 2025; flags and loan trouble share causes.

findings.title: Loans went bad 3.2x as often with 'Balance trending down'
findings.statement: Real outcomes, not simulation: among the 682 accounts with a loan, 28% of the 81 flagged 'Balance trending down' ended with the loan in trouble (status B or D) versus 9% of the other 601.
findings.caveat: Small groups for some flags; loan status is a snapshot at end of 2025; flags and loan trouble share causes.

findings.title: Loans went bad 3.9x as often with 'Uneven income'
findings.statement: Real outcomes, not simulation: among the 682 accounts with a loan, 20% of the 264 flagged 'Uneven income' ended with the loan in trouble (status B or D) versus 5% of the other 418.
findings.caveat: Small groups for some flags; loan status is a snapshot at end of 2025; flags and loan trouble share causes.

findings.title: Failing the simulated layoff lines up with real loan trouble
findings.statement: Borrowers who fail the simulated six-month layoff saw the loan go bad 14% of the time (454 accounts) versus 5% for those who survive it (228).
findings.caveat: The runway formula counts the loan payment inside spending, so part of this is mechanical.

findings.title: Balance sliding flag predicts significantly reduced layoff survival
findings.statement: Accounts flagged with balance_sliding (n = 493) have a six-month layoff survival rate of 34.7% compared to 68.2% for accounts without the flag, representing a 33.5 percentage point reduction in survival.
findings.caveat: Accounts with sliding balances also have lower median cash buffers (13,748 vs 24,223) and higher spending ratios (0.997 vs 0.910), which partly drives the lower survival.

findings.title: Prior weathered income drop strongly predicts layoff survival
findings.statement: Accounts flagged as weathered_before (n = 113) achieve a 92.0% six-month layoff survival rate compared to 63.8% for unflagged accounts, a 28.2 percentage point advantage.
findings.caveat: Accounts with the weathered_before flag also maintain lower median spending ratios (0.782 vs 0.921) and higher cash buffers (29,236 vs 22,133).

findings.title: Inflow volatility negatively correlates with layoff runway and survival
findings.statement: Inflow volatility (income_cv) has a Spearman correlation of -0.227 with layoff runway, with accounts in the lowest volatility quartile (<= 0.176, n = 1125) reaching an 85.2% layoff survival rate compared to 54.6% for the highest quartile (> 0.446, n = 1125).
findings.caveat: Income volatility correlates with higher spending ratios (spearman = 0.324), which contributes to reduced runway.

findings.title: Fee bleed flag counterintuitively associates with high layoff survival due to low base spending
findings.statement: Accounts flagged with fee_bleed (n = 310) achieve a 96.8% layoff survival rate compared to 62.1% for unflagged accounts, representing a 34.7 percentage point increase in survival.
findings.caveat: This counterintuitive result occurs because fee_bleed accounts have low absolute monthly spending (median S = 1,395 vs 8,144) and a low spending ratio (0.658 vs 0.930), so bank fees form a larger share of outflow while their buffer covers many months of spending.

findings.title: Pension-dependent households show near-total six-month layoff survival
findings.statement: Accounts flagged as pension_dependent (n = 740) achieve a 98.8% six-month layoff survival rate compared to 57.8% for non-pension accounts, a 41.0 percentage point difference.
findings.caveat: Pension-dependent accounts have lower median inflows (3,530 vs 9,468) but maintain much lower spending ratios (0.678 vs 0.946), extending their financial runway.

findings.title: Loan stress drastically reduces layoff survival despite average buffer size
findings.statement: Accounts flagged with loan_stress (n = 103) have a six-month layoff survival rate of only 28.2% compared to 65.4% for unflagged accounts, representing a 37.2 percentage point drop.
findings.caveat: Despite having similar median cash buffers to unflagged accounts (23,023 vs 22,306), loan-stressed households spend more than their inflow (median spending ratio 1.009 vs 0.916), accelerating buffer depletion under a shock.

findings.title: Older account owners demonstrate higher six-month layoff survival
findings.statement: Account owner age has a Spearman correlation of 0.208 with layoff runway, with owners aged 57.2 to 81 (n = 1120) achieving an 84.5% layoff survival rate compared to 55.7% for those aged 43.8 to 57.2 (n = 1129).
findings.caveat: Older account owners are more likely to be retired or receiving pensions, which correlates with lower spending ratios.

findings.title: Historical maximum drawdown share strongly predicts layoff survival
findings.statement: Max drawdown share (max_drawdown_share) strongly negatively correlates with layoff runway (Spearman = -0.621), with accounts in the lowest drawdown quartile (<= 0.433, n = 1125) achieving a 95.3% layoff survival rate compared to 26.2% for the highest quartile (> 1.17, n = 1125).
findings.caveat: Max drawdown share is defined relative to cash buffer B, so large historical balance dips inherently reflect depleted reserves.

summary: Beyond absolute balance size, structural spending habits and demographic factors heavily govern household resilience during a six-month income shock. Pensioners and households with low inflow volatility exhibit exceptionally high survival rates, whereas households experiencing balance sliding, high historical drawdowns, or heavy loan stress face rapid reserve depletion. Counterintuitively, accounts flagged for fee bleed show high survival due to low baseline monthly spending relative to their cash buffers.
best_finding: Pension-dependent households show near-total six-month layoff survival

baseline_findings.title: Loans went bad 11.6x as often with 'Goes negative on timing, not shortage'
baseline_findings.statement: Among the 682 accounts with a loan, 100% of the 19 flagged 'Goes negative on timing, not shortage' saw the loan go bad (status B or D) versus 9% of the rest.
baseline_findings.caveat: Real outcomes, not simulation; small groups, and the loan status is a snapshot at end of 2025.

baseline_findings.title: Loans went bad 25.4x as often with 'Paying penalty interest for going under'
baseline_findings.statement: Among the 682 accounts with a loan, 90% of the 60 flagged 'Paying penalty interest for going under' saw the loan go bad (status B or D) versus 4% of the rest.
baseline_findings.caveat: Real outcomes, not simulation; small groups, and the loan status is a snapshot at end of 2025.

baseline_findings.title: I / district average salary spreads survival by 62 points
baseline_findings.statement: Lowest quartile of inflow_vs_district_salary (-0.001 to 0.564) survives 95% of the time; highest quartile (2.25 to 8.22) 33%.
baseline_findings.caveat: Quartile spread; not adjusted for income.

baseline_findings.title: bank fees and penalty interest / outflow spreads survival by 59 points
baseline_findings.statement: Lowest quartile of fee_share (-0.001 to 0.000555) survives 36% of the time; highest quartile (0.00229 to 0.0126) 96%.
baseline_findings.caveat: Quartile spread; not adjusted for income.

baseline_findings.title: Flag 'Spending close to income' moves layoff survival by -53 points
baseline_findings.statement: 1847 accounts with 'Spending close to income' survive six months on 55% income 33% of the time versus 86% for the other 2653.
baseline_findings.caveat: Flags correlate with income and buffer; this is a difference, not a cause.
